extracted.intended_audience: general readers, naturalists, gardeners, and amateur botanists interested in plant behavior and child-development observations
extracted.subtask_description: A popular-science magazine-style treatment explaining the behaviors, classifications, and mechanisms of climbing plants (and related observational notes on early speech development), aimed at informed lay readers and gardeners. Emphasizes careful observation, simple experiments, models, and classification for explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily verbatim recording of infant speech
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have been in the habit of setting down daily on paper every expression, every sound that could be represented in writing, uttered by a child during the first two years," (use daily records as basis for a history of speech growth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a daily, runnable log of every representable vocalization/utterance for the first two years to provide factual basis for analysis and later publication; use the collected facts to derive patterns of speech development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for imitation when inferring inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is extremely hard to exclude the influence of imitation from the child ... and, when it is not excluded, to separate what is acquired by it from what is inherited."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying origins of faculties (e.g., speech), explicitly consider and try to control for imitation; avoid concluding a trait is wholly acquired or wholly inherited without isolating imitation effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document the developmental sequence and timing of speech phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe and record the sequence: early vowel-sounds, reflexive cries with distinctive tones, first consonants (e.g., m in seventh week), imitation onset, increasing articulation across half-years, comprehension preceding production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record timings (weeks/months) and qualitative changes (vowels → babbling → first consonants → connected phrases), noting comprehension vs production differences and parrot-like repetition versus understood usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative pathology to illuminate development
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare childish speech defects with lapses in grown persons after sickness — "we shall discover parallels of uncommon interest and astonishing completeness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies between developmental stages and pathological adult states to hypothesize about underlying mechanisms; identify corresponding faults and infer functional similarities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize direct observation and exceptions over prevailing theory
rubrics_metrics.description: "My present purpose has simply been to sketch the fundamental conditions ... independently of the theories of the day" and "It is by looking to exceptions that the key to a problem is often found."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base accounts on careful observation; deliberately seek and study exceptions as a method to understand general rules; present fundamental conditions even if they challenge contemporary theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish twiners from non-twiners in classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Climbers are "divided roughly into those which twine and those which do not twine; twiners ... climb by winding spirally round [a stick]" while non-twiners seize neighboring objects with hooks, adhering roots, or tendrils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying climbing plants, explicitly separate twining species from those that use hooks/tendrils/roots; this distinction has practical horticultural importance (wrong supports lead to failed cultivation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe and quantify revolving (swinging) movement of twining shoots
rubrics_metrics.description: Young twining shoots exhibit a revolving movement: "its tip is constantly traveling round and round ... making on an average, in warm August weather, one revolution in two hours."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make time-series observations to measure direction, regularity, and period of rotation; record how shoot-tip orientation changes over hours to document the searching movement that leads to twining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple physical models (rope, flexible rod) to explain twining
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogies: a swinging rope curling round a rod illustrates how a revolving shoot curls around a stick; a flexible rod model shows how unequal growth on sides produces revolving motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ accessible mechanical analogies and simple models to reason about plant movement (rope for curling, flexible rod for unequal-growth-induced bending) and to communicate mechanisms to lay audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note and test support-thickness limitations of twiners
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is a peculiarity of twining plants that they can only ascend moderately thin supports" — e.g., scarlet-runner climbs string or thin sticks but fails on thick trunks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimentally test supports of varying diameters to determine the effective range twiners can grip; relate ecological/fitness advantages (raising to light vs wasting growth on thick trunks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute movement to unequal growth and model growth-region changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Plant movements are produced by unequal growth: "one half of an organ growing in length quicker than the opposite half"; changing the region of quickest growth produces the revolving motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments or models to link differential growth rates across stem sides to curvature and rotation; document temporal changes in the region of fastest growth to explain spiraling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study handedness and other exceptions to understand mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions remain: "why every single hop-plant in a field twines like a left-handed screw ... nor why some species are divided into right- and left-handed individuals."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and analyze exceptions (handedness, reversal of spiral) systematically; use such anomalies as focal points for further experimental or comparative research to reveal causal factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use manipulative experiments (cuttings, transplants, shaking) to probe sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Twining organization is delicate: cut branches in water revolved in ~20 hours vs 2–3 hours on plant; moving a potted plant (slight shaking) can stop revolving movement temporarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform controlled manipulations (cutting, transplanting, mechanical disturbance) and measure their effects on rotation rate and twining behavior to assess sensitivity of the internal mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify and recognize multiple climbing methods and their combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Four different methods often encountered: twining, leaf-climbing, tendril-climbing, and root-climbing; some species (e.g., Bignonia) combine multiple methods, including hook-climbers and adhesive-root climbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing species, enumerate all climbing mechanisms present, note transitions during development (e.g., tendril → leaf climber), and explain functional differences and adaptive contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and test leaf/tendril sensitivity with small stimuli
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaf-stalks can be excited by very slight touches: "a loop of string weighing only one-sixteenth of a grain" or even paint crust can induce bending; terminal leaflet is often most sensitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use graded small stimuli (tiny weights, light touches, painted marks) to quantify sensitivity thresholds and response times for leaf-stalk or tendril curvature; map sensitivity across leaflet regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test tendril choice and adhesion preferences experimentally
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendrils may prefer darkness to light and show selective adhesion behavior: they curled around blackened glass/zinc then recoiled, but ultimately embraced rugged bark, swelled tips, and secreted a sticky cement forming adhesive disks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry out choice experiments (varied textures, materials, light/dark setups) to observe tendril preferences; monitor ensuing morphological changes (swelling, adhesive secretion) to document attachment strategies.
